questions.text: At a fixed pretraining compute budget, what trade-off do compute-optimal scaling laws help choose?

options.A: The split between attention heads and output vocabulary, regardless of data.
options.B: The split between training loss and test labels, regardless of model size.
options.C: The balance between parameter count and number of training tokens.
options.D: The balance between prompt length and output temperature during sampling.

questions.explanation: Training compute is approximately 6ND, so allocating a fixed budget requires balancing model parameters N and training tokens D.

questions.text: Why might a model intended to serve a very large volume of inference tokens be trained smaller and for more tokens than a pretraining-compute-only optimum suggests?

options.A: A smaller model always reaches zero loss if it sees enough tokens.
options.B: Extra training can improve a smaller model while reducing recurring inference cost.
options.C: More training tokens eliminate the need to store model weights at inference.
options.D: A smaller model makes training compute independent of the number of tokens.

questions.explanation: Accounting for repeated serving costs can favor more training of a smaller model, trading additional training expense for lower inference cost.
D=C/(6N), so halving N doubles D at fixed C.
